topic: Decision Making to Improve Financial Performance
subject: business-studies

items.title: ROCE compares like with like across firm sizes
items.claim: A firm has operating profit of £2 million, total assets of £15 million and current liabilities of £5 million. What is ROCE?
items.reveal_title: Operating profit divided by capital employed
items.reveal:
Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = £15m - £5m = £10m. ROCE = £2m / £10m = 20%.

ROCE is the most commonly cited single profitability measure in UK A-level. It is benchmarked against the cost of capital — if a firm consistently earns less than its weighted cost of capital, it is destroying shareholder value. UK FTSE 100 firms have averaged 10-15% ROCE over the last decade.
items.why: Absolute profit figures don't tell you whether capital was well used. A £2m profit from £10m of capital is 20%; the same profit from £100m of capital is 2%.

items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: Just-in-time becomes a vulnerability under shock
items.claim: Toyota pioneered just-in-time inventory. What happened to Toyota production during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: Toyota's global production fell by around 800,000 vehicles because a single supplier of microcontrollers (Renesas) was damaged

items.reveal:
Renesas's Naka factory in Ibaraki produced ~30% of automotive microcontrollers globally. After the 11 March 2011 earthquake, Toyota's worldwide output dropped sharply through to mid-2011. After Tohoku, Toyota mandated suppliers to map upstream dependencies and hold buffer stocks for critical components — partially abandoning pure JIT.

The 2020-22 COVID semiconductor shortages repeated the lesson industry-wide.
items.why: Lean optimises against ordinary variation. It does not optimise against catastrophic disruption — and the same firms that pioneered it have had to add 'just-in-case' buffers.
